column1: Why define a user-defined type instead of keeping separate low-level values?
column2:
A type groups a domain concept with its representation and meaningful operations. It can make intent clearer and help prevent invalid combinations of data; abstraction does not inherently require extra runtime overhead.

struct Point {
    double x;
    double y;
};
Point position{2.0, 3.0}; // one concept, not unrelated doubles

column1: What is the difference between struct and class for member access?
column2:
They provide the same class mechanisms, including constructors, methods, and access control. Members are public by default in a struct and private by default in a class. Explicit public/private declarations override the defaults.

struct A { int value; }; // public
class B { int value; };  // private
// A struct can also have private members and methods.

column1: When do you use . versus -> to access a member?
column2:
Use . through an object or reference, and -> through a pointer. For a built-in pointer, p->member is equivalent to (*p).member and requires a valid object.

struct Point { int x; };
Point point{3};
Point& ref = point;
Point* ptr = &point;
point.x = 4;
ref.x = 5;
ptr->x = 6; // same as (*ptr).x = 6

column1: Why does a function that initializes or modifies an existing object take a non-const reference?
column2:
A non-const reference gives the function access to the caller's original object without copying it. A by-value parameter is a separate object; modifying its own fields does not update the original fields.

struct Point { int x; };
void SetX(Point& point, int x) { point.x = x; }
Point p{0};
SetX(p, 7); // p.x becomes 7

column1: Why separate a class interface from its representation?
column2:
The public interface defines supported operations; private representation hides storage details. This lets methods preserve consistency and allows internal changes without changing how callers use the type. Private alone does not guarantee correct methods.

class Buffer {
public:
    void Append(char value);
    std::size_t Size() const;
private:
    std::vector<char> data_;
};
// Callers use Append/Size, not data_.

column1: What does a constructor do, and how is it named?
column2:
A constructor initializes an object when it is created. It has the class name and no return type. It can require the information needed to create a usable object, avoiding a separate initialization call.

struct Point {
    Point(int initialX) : x{initialX} {}
    int x;
};
Point point{7}; // constructor initializes x
// Point missing; // error: no zero-argument constructor

column1: Does declaring a constructor automatically initialize every scalar member to a known value?
column2:
No. The constructor or a default member initializer must initialize scalar members when a known value is needed. For this ordinary local object, the omitted int member has an indeterminate value; reading it is undefined behavior in C++20.

struct Counter {
    Counter() {}
    int count; // omitted from initialization
};
Counter counter;
// Reading counter.count here is undefined behavior.
// int count = 0; would supply a default member initializer.

column1: How does a constructor member initializer list differ from assignments in its body?
column2:
Members are initialized before the constructor body begins. The list after : specifies their initialization; statements in the body act on members afterward. Reference members must be bound during initialization, not assigned later.

struct View {
    int& value;
    View(int& source) : value{source} {}
};
// value = source in the body would not initialize the reference.

column1: What are () and {} called when initializing a member in a constructor?
column2:
size(n) uses direct-initialization; size{n} uses direct-list-initialization. Both can appear in the member initializer list after :. That list is not std::initializer_list. For class members, braces can select an initializer_list constructor and change the meaning.

struct Example {
    std::vector<int> values;
    Example() : values{3, 7} {} // two elements: 3, 7
    // Example() : values(3, 7) {} // three elements: 7, 7, 7
};
// Parentheses: ()   Braces: {}

column1: What are data members, function members, and type members?
column2:
Data members hold state; function members provide operations; type members declare nested types or aliases. A type declaration itself does not add per-object storage. Public nested types can be named using Class::Type.

class Buffer {
public:
    using SizeType = std::size_t; // type member
    SizeType Size() const;       // function member
private:
    SizeType size_ = 0;          // data member
};
Buffer::SizeType count = 3;

column1: Why would an element-access operator return T& instead of T?
column2:
Returning T& gives access to the actual element, enabling both reading and assignment through the result. Returning T gives a copy instead. In either case, the function must implement any required bounds checks itself.

// Inside a class whose elem points to its elements:
double& operator[](int index) { return elem[index]; }
// Then v[0] = 3.5 changes the stored element.
// No bounds check is provided by this implementation.

column1: How can a vector-like object keep a fixed size while its element count changes?
column2:
The object is a fixed-size handle containing metadata such as a pointer and a count. Elements occupy separate storage. Changing their number changes the count and possibly the allocation, not sizeof the handle. sizeof does not include separately allocated elements.

struct Handle {
    double* elem;
    std::size_t size;
};
// sizeof(Handle) includes fields and possible padding,
// not size * sizeof(double) bytes of external storage.

column1: Do a vector-like handle and its elements have to occupy the same storage region?
column2:
No. An ordinary local handle typically lives on the stack, while its dynamically allocated elements live separately on the free store. The handle itself can also be allocated dynamically; its type does not force stack placement.

std::vector<double> local(6); // local handle, dynamic elements
auto owner = std::make_unique<std::vector<double>>(6);
// The second vector object is dynamically allocated too.
// These are typical physical layouts; optimization can change storage.

column1: Does leaving a scope automatically release an array created with raw new[]?
column2:
No. Dynamic allocation lifetime is independent of the allocating block. Destroying a raw pointer does not release the array it points to. The owner must arrange cleanup; standard containers normally manage their own element storage.

int* data = nullptr;
{
    data = new int[3]{};
} // array still exists
data[0] = 7;
delete[] data; // releases the array; data is now dangling
